# Code review iteration

Reviewed the whole repository at commit `6a33365 2020-06-05`: all 8 Go files (`tracer.go`, `caller.go`, `context.go` and their tests, `example_test.go`, `helper_test.go`), `go.mod`, `Makefile`, `.golangci.yml`, `.travis.yml`, `githooks/`, and `README.md`. Review angle: correctness, concurrency, API design, and how the 2020-era decisions hold up against the Go 1.26-era ecosystem, in preparation for modernization. Review was done by reading only — no builds, tests, or linters were run. `.github/issues/` and `.github/roadmap/` were ignored as offline backlog dumps. No previous review files existed (`.github/reviews/` was absent), so all findings below are new.

Severity: **Crit** / **High** / **Med** / **Low** / **Nit**.
Class: `correctness` · `security` · `concurrency` · `perf` · `api` · `idiom` · `modern` · `test` · `build` · `docs`.

## 1. Trace and Call are not safe for concurrent use

Anchor: tracer.go:23-38 (`Trace.Start`), tracer.go:105-119 (`Call.Checkpoint`).

```go
if len(trace.stack) == cap(trace.stack) {
	trace.allocates++
}
trace.stack = append(trace.stack, call)
```

The whole point of the library is to inject a single `*Trace` into a request context and call `Fetch(ctx).Start()` from every function down the call chain — that is exactly what the README and `example_test.go` demonstrate. But `Trace.stack` and `Call.checkpoints` are mutated with plain slice appends, with no synchronization and no documented single-goroutine contract. The moment a handler fans out work (`errgroup`, `go func` per backend call — bog-standard in today's HTTP services), two goroutines race on the same slice header: lost calls, a corrupted stack, and an instant `-race` failure. A tracing library whose canonical use case is request-scoped context propagation must either be goroutine-safe or scream that it is not.

**Fix.** Add a `sync.Mutex` to `Trace` (guarding `stack`/`allocates`) and to `Call` (guarding `checkpoints`/`allocates`), and take it in `Start`, `Checkpoint`, `Stop`, and `String`. An uncontended mutex costs nanoseconds — noise next to the two `time.Now()` calls already on every path, and the project's own benchmarks can prove it. If lock-free is a hard requirement, the alternative is to document the single-goroutine constraint in the package doc and on every method, but for this API shape safety is the right default.

## 2. Caller panics when the runtime lookup fails

Anchor: caller.go:13-19.

```go
pc := make([]uintptr, 1)
runtime.Callers(skip, pc)
f := runtime.FuncForPC(pc[0])
file, line := f.FileLine(pc[0])
```

The return value of `runtime.Callers` is ignored. When `skip` exceeds the actual stack depth, zero frames are written, `pc[0]` stays `0`, and `runtime.FuncForPC(0)` returns nil per its contract ("or else nil") — so `f.FileLine` dereferences a nil pointer and panics. `Caller` is an exported function that documents passing arbitrary skip values (`Caller(2)` in its own doc comment), so any user wrapping it in a helper with a miscounted skip gets a runtime panic instead of a zero value. For a library whose selling point is "won't panic" nil-safety (see `Fetch`/`Start`/`Stop`), this is an inconsistent and avoidable crash.

**Fix.** Check the frame count and bail out with a zero `CallerInfo`:

```go
var pcs [1]uintptr
if runtime.Callers(skip, pcs[:]) == 0 {
	return CallerInfo{}
}
frame, _ := runtime.CallersFrames(pcs[:1]).Next()
return CallerInfo{frame.Entry, frame.Function, frame.File, frame.Line}
```

This also resolves finding 4 in the same stroke.

## 3. Toolchain, CI, and lint setup are six years stale

Anchor: go.mod:3, .travis.yml:1-49, .golangci.yml:1-14, Makefile:5-33.

The repo is frozen in mid-2020 across every axis:

- `go 1.11` in `go.mod` pins the language to a pre-modules-maturity version; the current era is Go 1.26. No `toolchain` directive.
- CI is Travis (`.travis.yml`, README badge on travis-ci.com) with a 1.11–1.14 matrix. Travis ended free OSS builds in 2021 — this pipeline is dead, so the project effectively has **no CI at all**. The file also carries an encrypted Slack token for a defunct integration.
- `.golangci.yml` enables `structcheck`, `varcheck`, and `deadcode` — deprecated in golangci-lint v1.49 (2022), long removed, and subsumed by `unused`. The config schema itself has moved on (v2 requires `version: "2"`; top-level `linters.fast` is gone). Current golangci-lint will reject this file.
- The Makefile is built around obsolete knobs: `GO111MODULE=on` (default since 1.16), `GOFLAGS=-mod=vendor` with no `vendor/` directory in sight, `GOPROXY=direct` (bypasses the module proxy and checksum DB for no benefit), `go get -d` (the flag is a no-op since Go 1.18), and version sniffing for Go 1.11–1.13.
- Nothing modern is present: no GitHub Actions, no Dependabot/Renovate, no `govulncheck`, no CodeQL, no release automation.

**Fix.** Migration outline: (1) bump `go.mod` to a supported directive (e.g. `go 1.25`) and drop the vendor-mode flags; (2) replace Travis with a GitHub Actions workflow — test matrix on `stable`/`oldstable` with `-race` and coverage upload, plus a `govulncheck` step; (3) delete `.travis.yml` including the dead Slack secret; (4) rewrite `.golangci.yml` for v2 (`version: "2"`, drop removed linters, enable the current `staticcheck`/`govet`/`revive`/`gocritic` set); (5) add `dependabot.yml` for `github-actions` and `gomod` ecosystems; (6) regenerate the Makefile from the current octomation/makefiles template or trim it to the handful of targets actually used.

## 4. Caller reports the wrong line and ignores inlining

Anchor: caller.go:17.

`pc[0]` returned by `runtime.Callers` is a *return address*, i.e. it points at the instruction after the call. Feeding it straight into `f.FileLine(pc[0])` therefore reports the line *following* the call site, and `CallerInfo.Line` is off by one line (or more, with multi-line statements) in every trace. Moreover, the `runtime.Callers` documentation explicitly discourages exactly this pattern: iterating the raw PCs with `FuncForPC` "cannot account for inlining or return program counter adjustment" — and mid-stack inlining has been on by default since Go 1.12, two releases after this code was written. Under a modern toolchain the reported function name can be misattributed when frames are inlined; `caller_test.go:20` already hedges around a 1.11-vs-1.12 naming difference instead of fixing the root cause.

**Fix.** Use `runtime.CallersFrames`, which adjusts return PCs to call PCs and expands inlined frames correctly — see the code in finding 2. `frame.Function`/`frame.File`/`frame.Line` replace the `FuncForPC` triple one-for-one; only `Entry` semantics need a note (for an inlined frame it is the entry of the physical function).

## 5. String renders garbage durations for unstopped calls

Anchor: tracer.go:62.

```go
builder.WriteString(call.stop.Sub(call.start).String())
```

If a call was started but never stopped, `call.stop` is the zero `time.Time`, and `stop.Sub(start)` saturates to the minimum `time.Duration` — the trace prints `-2562047h47m16.854775808s`. This is not a corner case for this library: its stated motivation (README, Motivation section) is diagnosing *aborted* requests (`write: broken pipe`), and a middleware that flushes the trace when a request dies mid-flight will hit exactly this — in-flight calls that were never `Stop()`ed. The one situation the library was built for produces the most nonsensical output.

**Fix.** In `String`, branch on `call.stop.IsZero()`: render `time.Since(call.start)` with an explicit marker, e.g. `call FetchData: 1.19ms (in progress)`. Same consideration applies if `Stop` was called before any work — a zero duration is fine, but a negative one never is.

## 6. Labels are accepted but silently discarded

Anchor: tracer.go:23-32, tracer.go:105-118, struct fields at tracer.go:86 and tracer.go:139.

```go
var id string
if len(labels) > 0 {
	id, labels = labels[0], labels[1:]
}
```

The doc comments advertise `Start("id", "labelX", "labelY")` and `Checkpoint("id", "labelX", "labelY")`, and the remaining labels are dutifully stored in `Call.labels` / `Checkpoint.labels` — unexported fields that `String()` never renders and no accessor exposes. Every label a user passes is dead weight: allocated, retained, and invisible. On top of that, the "first variadic element is secretly the ID" convention is a trap — `Start("labelX")` quietly turns a label into an ID, and there is no way to pass labels without an ID.

**Fix.** Decide which way to go and be honest about it: either render labels in `String()` and add accessors so the data is reachable, or delete the `labels` fields and change the signatures to an explicit `Start(id string)` / `Checkpoint(id string)`. The README already declares the library is not BC-safe across major releases, so a v2 signature cleanup is available. Do not keep accepting parameters that go nowhere.

## 7. Inject leaks internal representation and Trace has no read API

Anchor: context.go:23-25.

```go
func Inject(ctx context.Context, stack []*Call) context.Context {
	return context.WithValue(ctx, key{}, &Trace{stack: stack})
}
```

The only thing a caller legitimately controls here is the initial *capacity*, yet the API demands the internal storage itself — hence the `make([]*tracer.Call, 0, 10)` boilerplate copy-pasted through the README and examples, and the ability to pre-seed a trace with arbitrary foreign `*Call` values (including nils, which would then panic `String()` — nothing validates them). Meanwhile the read side is a dead end: `Trace` exposes exactly one output, `String()`. There is no way to get calls, durations, or checkpoints as data, so the trace cannot feed structured logging or be bridged into a real tracing backend (OpenTelemetry spans, for instance) — which is where a 2026 consumer would want to send it.

**Fix.** Change the constructor to hide the representation — `Inject(ctx context.Context, capacity int) context.Context` (or a functional option) — and add a structured read API, e.g. a `Calls()` method returning copies with exported ID/Caller/Start/Stop/Checkpoints. Keep `String()` as a convenience formatter on top of the structured form.

## 8. Example test is timing-sensitive by construction

Anchor: example_test.go:100-108, with real sleeps at example_test.go:64-96.

```go
raw = regexp.MustCompile(`Handle (.+): (\d{2}\.\d+ms)`).ReplaceAllString(raw, "Handle $1: 12.345678ms")
...
raw = regexp.MustCompile(`FetchData: (\d\.\d+ms)`).ReplaceAllString(raw, "FetchData: 1.234567ms")
```

`Example()` asserts on output stabilized by regexes that hard-code the *digit shape* of real measured durations: `Handle` must land in 10–99ms, `FetchData` in 1–9ms, `StoreIntoDatabase` in 10–99ms. The handler really sleeps (`time.Sleep` × ~26ms total), so on a loaded CI runner any sleep stretching past a decade boundary (FetchData ≥ 10ms, Handle ≥ 100ms) makes its regex silently not match, the raw duration leaks into the output, and the Example fails. This is the classic sleep-based flaky test, made worse by the silent-fallthrough normalizer. It also caps how aggressive the `make test` timeout (`-timeout 1s`) can be.

**Fix.** Normalize any duration token wholesale — one regex like `\d+(\.\d+)?(ns|µs|ms|s)` replaced with a constant — so correctness of the *structure* is asserted and the timings are irrelevant. Better still, make time injectable (a package-level `now func() time.Time` hook or a clock field) and drop the sleeps entirely; the example then becomes deterministic and instant.

## 9. README badges and links are dead

Anchor: README.md:119-132.

- `build.page`/`build.icon` point at travis-ci.com — the service no longer runs this project's builds (see finding 3), so the badge is dead or permanently red.
- `awesome.icon` loads from `cdn.rawgit.com` — RawGit was sunset in October 2019 and is fully offline; the badge image is broken.
- The Integration section links `github.com/golang/go/wiki/Modules`; the Go wiki moved to `go.dev/wiki`, and in 2026 a "how to use go modules" primer is noise anyway.
- `design.page` points to a Notion workspace page — worth verifying it is still public before advertising it as "a full description of the idea".

**Fix.** Swap the build badge for a GitHub Actions workflow badge once finding 3 lands, source the awesome badge from `awesome.re`/shields.io, update or drop the wiki link, and re-verify the Notion link (or move the design doc into the repo, where it cannot rot).

## 10. Assorted pre-modules-era idioms

Anchor: example_test.go:101, caller_test.go:24, tracer.go:17-22.

Small things a modern linter pass would flag, batched here:

- `strings.Replace(raw, "tracer_test.", "", -1)` (example_test.go:101) → `strings.ReplaceAll`, available since Go 1.12.
- Loop-variable copies `tc := test` / `tc := bm` (caller_test.go:24, caller_test.go:54) have been unnecessary since Go 1.22 changed loop-variable scoping.
- Dot imports `. "github.com/kamilsk/tracer"` in every test file — staticcheck ST1001 discourages them even in tests; a plain `tracer.` prefix costs nothing.
- Doc comments use pre-Go 1.19 formatting conventions: two-space indented code blocks and trailing bare `//` lines (tracer.go:17-22 and siblings). `gofmt` ≥ 1.19 reformats doc comments; the indented examples would be better as compilable `Example*` functions that show up rendered and tested on pkg.go.dev.

**Fix.** Mechanical: bump the toolchain (finding 3), run `gofmt` and a current golangci-lint config, and apply the autofixes; convert the doc-comment snippets to testable examples while touching the files.
